newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS - Ringgit falls below 2.53/dlr on rumours, technicals.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ringgit falls below 2.53/dlr on rumours, technicals.

text.p: U.S. funds and speculators combined rumours and technical reasons to pull down the ringgit sharply to below 2.53 per dollar, dealers said on Wednesday.
By 1130 GMT, the ringgit had dipped to 2.5305/15 a dollar in London after closing at 2.5250/60 in Kuala Lumpur and against 2.5135/40 at close of trading on Tuesday.
It has lost over 275 points from around 2.5025 on Friday.

The dealers said some large speculators based in Singapore and London were testing the tolerance levels of Bank Negara Malaysia, the central bank, which usually intervenes to smooth sharp fluctuations in the currency.
"They are testing how long Bank Negara will tolerate this sell down and they are using rumours to do that," said a dealer with a U.S. bank in Singapore.
"At least $300 to $400 (million) was bought today," the dealer said.
Dealers said it was widely rumoured that Bank Negara was comfortable with the decline of the ringgit to between 2.52 and 2.53 per dollar.
Bank Negara did not immediately have a comment.

Dealers said the market also used an overnight report from London that the U.S. was seeking sanctions against Malaysia's national oil firm Petronas for its involvement in an Iranian oil project to push the ringgit lower.

The report was used despite U.S. Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary's comment later that the Clinton government would wait until after the November 5 presidential election to decide how it will enforce sanctions against Libya and Iran.
"The ringgit continues to be susceptible to rumours in the market as players search for excuses to sell the ringgit," research firm I.D.E.A. said in a comment late on Wednesday.
It said there was also talk about Bank Negara buying U.S. dollars at around 2.5180 per dollar level.
"Neither (of these reasons) look credible," I.D.E.A. said.

It said a firm ringgit would help keep imported inflation low as the central bank maintains a firm monetary policy and reduce value of imports, particularly against the Japanese yen, when the country is trying to cut its negative balance of payments. However, dealers predicted that the ringgit was likely to go down further unless there was profit-taking or a central bank intervention.

They said year-end requirement of dollars by Malaysian corporate sector, repatriation of profits by foreign investors, and government's forecast of large monthly trade deficits for the rest of the year in the Economic Report for 1996/97 were expected to pull down the ringgit.
"Once the 2.5180 per dollar resistance was broken, the market was more willing to hold dollars than before," said a senior dealer with a Malaysian bank in Kuala Lumpur.
He said beyond 2.5180, there was also a lot of unwinding of long ringgit positions against the Singapore dollar. "Even structured (portfolio) positions are being unwound," he said.

Another Malaysian foreign exchange dealer said it was possible that Bank Negara was having problems keeping down domestic interbank liquidity, which has several times threatened its tight monetary policy and forced it to intervene.
However, the interventions in the open market to mop up liquidity was becoming expensive, so Bank Negara may be allowing some of the short-term offshore funds to flow out, he said.
- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 8911)
